name: Pineal gland
function: Neuroendocrine circumventricular organ converting SCN-driven, sympathetic (superior cervical ganglion) noradrenergic signaling into nightly melatonin secretion — the hormonal signal of darkness that entrains circadian physiology; it calcifies after puberty and serves as the radiographic midline landmark.

afferent: Suprachiasmatic nucleus, via the paraventricular nucleus, intermediolateral column and superior cervical ganglion (sympathetic fibers)
Habenula and stria medullaris thalami fibers
efferent: Melatonin released into the systemic circulation and CSF (no blood-brain barrier)

bloodSupply: Medial posterior choroidal arteries (collicular/quadrigeminal region); venous drainage to the internal cerebral veins and great vein of Galen.

clinical.syndrome: Pineal region tumor with gaze palsy
clinical.findings: Germinomas and pineal parenchymal tumors compress the pretectal plate and aqueduct — upgaze palsy, light-near dissociation, lid retraction, convergence-retraction nystagmus (Parinaud syndrome) with hydrocephalus; see the syndrome browser entry.
clinical.note: mass effect, not a primary vascular syndrome

clinical.findings: Pinealectomy or sympathetic interruption (Horner syndrome, cervical cord injury) blunts nocturnal melatonin and disorganizes sleep phase.
Masses at the posterior third ventricle obstruct the cerebral aqueduct, causing headache, papilledema and gait failure before focal signs.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'
RadioGraphics 2019 — 'Midbrain, Pons, and Medulla: Anatomy and Syndromes'

name: Habenular nuclei
function: Limbic 'anti-reward' interface: the lateral habenula integrates stria-medullaris input from septum, hypothalamus and basal ganglia and suppresses dopaminergic (VTA/SNc) and serotonergic (raphe) activity — encoding negative reward prediction, aversion and pain expectation; the medial habenula relays to the interpeduncular nucleus for aversive behavioral control.

afferent: Stria medullaris thalami (septal nuclei, preoptic area, lateral hypothalamus)
Lateral pallidum (pallidohabenular fibers) and basal ganglia
Bed nucleus of the stria terminalis
efferent: Ventral tegmental area and substantia nigra pars compacta (inhibitory, lateral habenula)
Interpeduncular nucleus via the fasciculus retroflexus (medial habenula)

bloodSupply: Medial posterior choroidal artery (PCA branches) at the epithalamic dorsal midline.

clinical.findings: Lateral habenula hyperactivity is a robust correlate of major depression and helplessness in humans and animal models; habenula/fasciculus-retroflexus stimulation is an experimental treatment for refractory depression.
Tumors or infarcts at the dorsal midline interrupting the habenulo-interpeduncular pathway contribute to reward-processing disturbance and sleep-wake dysregulation.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 3rd ed., Ch. 'Limbic System: Homeostasis, Olfaction, Memory, and Emotion'

name: Stria medullaris thalami
function: Myelinated limbic afferent bundle sweeping along the dorsomedial border of the thalamus from the septal/preoptic region to the habenular nuclei — the principal input limb of the epithalamic circuit feeding the anti-reward system.

afferent: Septal nuclei and nucleus accumbens
Preoptic area and lateral hypothalamus
Bed nucleus of the stria terminalis and olfactory tubercle
efferent: Medial and lateral habenular nuclei (the habenular peduncle continues as the fasciculus retroflexus)

bloodSupply: Medial posterior choroidal branches of the PCA (dorsal thalamic/epithalamic margin).

clinical.findings: The bed-nucleus/stria-medullaris region is a deep-brain-stimulation target for treatment-resistant obsessive-compulsive disorder, reflecting its limbic-to-habenular relay role.
Tumor or infarct along the stria interrupts limbic-to-habenular traffic, contributing to emotional blunting and attention-memory deficits.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'

name: Posterior commissure
function: Dorsal midline fiber decussation at the entrance to the cerebral aqueduct that crosses pretectal and posterior thalamic fibers coordinating bilateral vertical gaze — most critically linking the riMLF and interstitial nucleus of Cajal of the two sides for upgaze and pupillomotor symmetry.

afferent: Pretectal nuclei (pupillomotor interneurons)
riMLF and interstitial nucleus of Cajal (vertical gaze fibers)
Posterior thalamic nuclei
efferent: Contralateral riMLF, interstitial nucleus of Cajal and oculomotor complex (bilateral vertical eye-movement coordination)

bloodSupply: Collicular/quadrigeminal branches of the PCA (P1/P2) and the medial posterior choroidal artery.

clinical.findings: Compression of the posterior commissure/pretectal region by pineal tumors or hydrocephalus abolishes coordinated upgaze and convergence and yields light-near dissociation; see the syndrome browser entry.
PCA-collicular-territory infarcts splitting the commissure produce vertical gaze palsy and skew deviation.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 3rd ed., Ch. 'Brainstem II: Eye Movements and Pupillary Control'

name: Subthalamic nucleus
function: Biconvex, lens-shaped excitatory hub of the indirect basal-ganglia pathway: glutamatergic STN neurons drive GPi/SNr output, raising the thalamocortical brake on movement; loss of this drive disinhibits the motor thalamus and releases violent involuntary movement. The hyperdirect cortex-STN loop also gates movement cancellation.

afferent: Lateral segment of the globus pallidus externa (indirect pathway)
Motor cortex via the hyperdirect (corticosubthalamic) pathway
Substantia nigra pars compacta (dopaminergic modulation)
efferent: Globus pallidus internus and substantia nigra pars reticulata (excitatory, glutamatergic)
Reciprocal projections back to the globus pallidus externa

bloodSupply: Small perforating branches of the posterior communicating artery and the anterior choroidal artery (rostral/lateral STN); P1/PCA perforators caudally.

clinical.findings: Contralateral wild, flinging movements of the proximal arm and leg after STN infarction or hemorrhage; typically worst at onset and improving over weeks, with dopamine-receptor blockers or tetrabenazine for severe cases; see the syndrome browser entry.
High-frequency STN stimulation is standard therapy for advanced Parkinson motor fluctuations; current spread into limbic/associative STN territory can induce impulsivity, hypomania or dyskinesia.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 3rd ed., Ch. 'Basal Ganglia', section 'Ansa Lenticularis, Lenticular Fasciculus, and the Fields of Forel'

name: Zona incerta
function: A rostrocaudal GABAergic sheet between the thalamus and the subthalamic nucleus, continuous with the thalamic reticular nucleus: it gates viscerosensory, cerebellar and basal-ganglia traffic — influencing saccades, arousal, blood pressure and tremor networks — and is traversed by the H1/H2 fasciculi.

afferent: Cerebellar nuclei (fastigial and interposed, via superior cerebellar peduncle collaterals)
Pretectum and spinal/trigeminal sensory inputs
Basal ganglia and motor cortex

bloodSupply: Posterior communicating and anterior choroidal perforators; thalamogeniculate/paramedian PCA branches caudally.

clinical.findings: ZI stimulation suppresses tremor comparably to VIM thalamotomy and is used as a DBS target; lesions or current spread can rarely provoke transient hemiballismus-like movements.
Subthalamic-region infarcts involving the zona incerta combine hemisensory loss, ataxia and involuntary movements (choreoathetosis or ballism).

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 3rd ed., Ch. 'Basal Ganglia', section 'Ansa Lenticularis, Lenticular Fasciculus, and the Fields of Forel'

name: Fields of Forel (H1/H2)
function: Fiber-field complex of the subthalamus: field H2 (lenticular fasciculus) carries pallidal output looping through the internal capsule, and field H1 (thalamic fasciculus) delivers it to the ventral anterior and ventral lateral nuclei — the final common route of basal-ganglia output to the motor thalamus, shared with cerebellothalamic fibers.
contextNote: Context record for the H1 (thalamic fasciculus) and H2 (lenticular fasciculus) white-matter zones medial to the zona incerta; drawn on plate-thalamus-mid and plate-coronal-midbrain. See also nuc-subthalamic and nuc-zona-incerta.

afferent: Globus pallidus internus via the ansa lenticularis and lenticular fasciculus (H2)
Dentate nucleus via the superior cerebellar peduncle (cerebellothalamic fibers share the field)
efferent: Ventral anterior and ventral lateral thalamic nuclei via the thalamic fasciculus (H1)

bloodSupply: Perforating branches of the posterior communicating and anterior choroidal arteries.

clinical.findings: Hemorrhage or stereotactic lesions across the H fields mimic pallidotomy — reduced contralateral rigidity with a risk of choreoballismic movements.
Targeted H1/H2 interruption was used historically for tremor and rigidity and remains a named landmark concept in functional-neurosurgery planning.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 3rd ed., Ch. 'Basal Ganglia', section 'Ansa Lenticularis, Lenticular Fasciculus, and the Fields of Forel'
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'

name: Third ventricle
function: The narrow midline CSF cavity between the paired thalami, extending from the lamina terminalis and optic chiasm to the pineal recess and aqueduct; its choroid plexus secretes CSF, the interventricular foramina of Monro drain both lateral ventricles into it, and its walls carry the midline thalamic nuclei and hypothalamus.

afferent: Lateral ventricles via the interventricular foramina of Monro

bloodSupply: Medial posterior choroidal artery (choroid plexus); walls supplied by circumferential PCA and anterior choroidal perforators.

clinical.syndrome: Colloid cyst of the third ventricle
clinical.findings: A foramen-of-Monro cyst traps the lateral ventricles — episodic headache, papilledema and gait failure; acute blockage can cause sudden deterioration or death.
Obstruction at the caudal third ventricle dilates the third and lateral ventricles (non-communicating hydrocephalus) with normal fourth ventricle.
Bilateral thalamic gliomas or hypothalamic tumors narrow the slit, presenting with hydrocephalus plus endocrine and visual deficits.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 3rd ed., Ch. 'Brain and Environs: Cranium, Ventricles, and Meninges'
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'

name: Cerebral aqueduct
function: The roughly 1.5 cm CSF conduit through the midbrain periaqueductal gray linking the third to the fourth ventricle beneath the colliculi; it is the narrowest CSF channel and the classic site of obstruction by tectal tumors, post-hemorrhagic webs or aqueductal stenosis.

afferent: Third ventricle at the plane of the posterior commissure
efferent: Fourth ventricle at the pontomesencephalic isthmus

bloodSupply: Paramedian and circumferential perforating branches of the PCA/SCA to the surrounding periaqueductal gray (no intrinsic choroid).

clinical.findings: Aqueduct obstruction (tectal glioma, post-hemorrhagic web, congenital stenosis) dilates the third and lateral ventricles with a normal fourth — headache, Parinaud signs and gait ataxia.
Lesions of the surrounding PAG (hemorrhage, demyelination) disturb pain modulation and the vertical-gaze centers flanking the duct.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 3rd ed., Ch. 'Brain and Environs: Cranium, Ventricles, and Meninges'
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 3rd ed., Ch. 'Brainstem III: Internal Structures and Vascular Supply'

name: Corpus callosum (context)
function: The great commissure linking the cerebral hemispheres, drawn as the sagittal-plate arch above the diencephalon; it forms the roof of the lateral ventricles and the superior boundary of the atlas scene.
contextNote: Context silhouette for the sagittal plate and 3D scene roof; not a diencephalic structure (hemisphere context).

afferent: Commissural fibers from cortical layers II/III of both hemispheres
efferent: Homotopic projections to the contralateral cortex

bloodSupply: Anterior cerebral artery (pericallosal branches) and posterior cerebral artery (splenial branches).

clinical.findings: Surgical callosal section isolates the hemispheres — the left hand acts independently and cannot name objects seen by the right hemisphere; callosal thinning also appears in ALS and developmental disorders.
Congenital absence elevates the third ventricle roof on sagittal imaging and may accompany hypothalamic dysregulation syndromes (e.g., episodic hypothermia).

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'

name: Internal capsule (context)
function: The fan-shaped white-matter plane carrying all thalamocortical and corticofugal traffic — anterior limb (frontopontine), genu (corticobulbar), posterior limb (corticospinal and somatosensory thalamocortical), retrolenticular (optic radiations) — framing the thalamus laterally on the thalamic-level plates; the thalamic reticular nucleus hugs its inner surface.
contextNote: Context silhouette on plate-thalamus-mid and plate-coronal-thalamus; see also the subthalamus records for the pallidal (H1/H2) fasciculi looping through it.

afferent: Thalamocortical radiations (VPL/VPM to S1; LGN to V1; VL/VA to motor cortex)
efferent: Corticospinal, corticobulbar and corticopontine fibers funnelling from the corona radiata

bloodSupply: Lenticulostriate branches of the MCA (genu/posterior limb), anterior choroidal artery (retrolenticular and inferior posterior limb), recurrent artery of Heubner (anterior limb).

clinical.findings: Small posterior-limb/genu infarcts give contralateral face-arm-leg weakness without cortical signs; larger capsular strokes add dense hemisensory loss and dysarthria-clumsy-hand syndrome.
Contralateral incongruous homonymous hemianopia from anterior-choroidal-territory infarction of the optic radiations.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 3rd ed., Ch. 'Corticospinal Tract and Other Motor Pathways'
Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 2nd ed., Ch. 'Diencephalon: Thalamus and Hypothalamus'

name: Lentiform nucleus (context silhouette)
function: Silhouette of the putamen and globus pallidus lateral to the internal capsule, shown on the transverse and coronal thalamic plates for orientation; the striatopallidal loops ending here gate movement through the ventral anterior and ventral lateral thalamus.
contextNote: Context silhouette; basal-ganglia detail is out of scope for v1 — see ctx-internal-capsule and the subthalamus records.

afferent: Striatal input to the globus pallidus (direct and indirect pathway convergence)
efferent: Pallidal output via the ansa lenticularis and lenticular fasciculus (H2) to the motor thalamus

bloodSupply: Lenticulostriate branches of the MCA; anterior choroidal artery supplies the inferior and posterior pallidum.

clinical.findings: Small deep infarcts or hemorrhages here produce pure motor or sensorimotor hemiparesis; larger putaminal bleeds cause gaze deviation and reduced consciousness.
Carbon-monoxide or manganese injury to the globus pallidus causes parkinsonism and dystonia — context for the basal-ganglia-thalamic loop the atlas teaches.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 3rd ed., Ch. 'Basal Ganglia'

name: Caudate nucleus (context silhouette)
function: C-shaped striatal silhouette along the lateral ventricle — head at the anterior limb of the internal capsule, body over the thalamus — drawn at the superior-anterior margin of the thalamic plates as striatal context.
contextNote: Context silhouette; see ctx-lenticular-nucleus and ctx-internal-capsule for adjacent context records.

afferent: Corticostriate fibers from prefrontal and associative cortex; nigrostriatal dopamine
efferent: Caudate projections to the globus pallidus externa and substantia nigra pars reticulata (indirect pathway entry)

bloodSupply: Medial lenticulostriate and anterior cerebral (recurrent artery of Heubner) perforators for the head; lateral lenticulostriate branches for the body.

clinical.findings: Head-of-caudate lacunes (Heubner territory) produce abulia, disinhibition and contralateral neglect, mimicking frontal-lobe lesions.
Progressive caudate volume loss underlies chorea and frontal-executive decline — visible on the coronal context silhouettes.

refs: Blumenfeld, Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases, 3rd ed., Ch. 'Basal Ganglia'
